title: How a Tsunami Races Across the Ocean
post_title: How a Tsunami Races Across the Ocean | QuantaTale
post_description: What sets off a tsunami, how it travels and how it behaves near shore, from NOAA and USGS. Sources: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/tsunami.html and United States Geological Survey https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-are-tsunamis #Science #ScienceFacts #QuantaTale
narration: What turns an underwater shake into a giant wave? Tsunamis are waves set off by undersea earthquakes or volcanic eruptions. Volcanoes, landslides and even atmospheric disturbances can also trigger them. Out in the deep ocean, the waves do not grow dramatically in height. The speed of a tsunami depends on ocean depth, not on distance from the source. As the ocean gets shallower toward land, they build up to greater and greater heights. Near shore, it behaves like an extremely fast tide that pushes much farther inland. And it usually arrives as several waves, not just one.
